title: Multi-agent orchestration without the chaos
linkedinPost:
40% of multi-agent AI pilots fail within 6 months of going live. The reason is almost never the model.

Gartner logged a 1,445% surge in multi-agent system inquiries in 18 months. Only 11–14% of those pilots have reached production at scale. The gap traces to 4 design decisions most teams skip.

No task decomposition → 2 agents with overlapping scope, both running, neither catching the error.

Implicit handoffs → raw text passed between agents, a formatting change in step 1 silently breaking step 4.

No oversight gates → pipelines running end-to-end with no human review before a credit decision hits a regulatory record.

No audit log as infrastructure → DORA and the EU AI Act (enforceable August 2026) require immutable, machine-readable trails. A log file is not an audit trail.

What I would actually do:

• Define typed JSON contracts for every handoff before writing a single prompt
• Add human gates at the 2–3 points where errors are hardest to reverse
• Build the audit log as a first-class pipeline output — Supabase with immutable timestamps
• Test failure scenarios at pipeline level: what happens when agent 2 breaks?
• Set revenue per employee targets by function, not pipeline efficiency metrics in isolation

Multi-agent orchestration raises revenue per employee when the system is designed to fail safely and scale predictably — not just to run.

Full piece + the Orchestration Discipline Model I use to structure every multi-agent build — link in comments.

mainEntity.name: What is multi-agent orchestration in simple terms?

acceptedAnswer.text: Multiple AI agents, each with a defined job, working together through validated handoffs to complete a task that no single agent could handle reliably alone. An orchestrator — human-designed or AI-driven — decides which agent runs when and what it receives.

mainEntity.name: How is multi-agent orchestration different from a single AI agent?

acceptedAnswer.text: A single agent reasons over the full task. Multi-agent orchestration decomposes it — each agent owns a smaller, more defined piece of work and passes a validated output to the next. This improves reliability and auditability at the cost of higher design complexity upfront.

mainEntity.name: What are the most common multi-agent orchestration failure modes?

acceptedAnswer.text: Overlapping agent scope, implicit (untyped) handoffs, missing human oversight gates, and no immutable audit logging. The majority of production failures in financial services trace to one of these four.

mainEntity.name: Does the EU AI Act apply to multi-agent orchestration systems in financial services?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes. Classification is based on what the system does, not its architecture. A pipeline producing credit decisions, fraud determinations, or customer eligibility outcomes is high-risk under Annex III, requiring human oversight capability, immutable audit trails, and documented incident testing.
